evidence.claim: The manuscript relies heavily on self-citations and lacks sufficient attribution to alternative or complementary analyses by other groups, particularly in Sec. 3.1.
evidence.excerpt: A substantial fraction of the references (Refs. 9, 10, 11, 19, 26, 27) are works co-authored by the contributor... alternative or complementary analyses of axion-photon conversion in SN progenitor or galactic fields by other groups deserve clearer attribution.

judge_panel.reason: The paper is a conference proceedings overview by the lead author, so self-citations are expected in this genre. However, in Sec. 3.1 the paper does cite several works by other groups (Refs. 20–26), including Meyer & Petrushevska, Crnogorčević et al., and Manzari et al., so the claim of lacking attribution is partially unfounded. The concern about balance is legitimate but highly subjective for a proceedings contribution.

Sec. 3.1 does attribute complementary work by other groups, e.g. "the non-observation of any signal by the SMM rules out values of the product of the coupling ... 13," "axion-photon conversions within the SN progenitor magnetic field may eventually dominate22," and "the analysis of gamma-ray bursts from more frequent extragalactic SNe ... was also employed in previous works to point out possible axion signatures 24,25."

The reviewer correctly points out that a substantial fraction of the bibliography (Refs. 9, 10, 11, 19, 26, 27) consists of works authored by the manuscript's sole author, making the critique about heavy self-citation and the need for broader attribution a valid editorial concern.

general.reason: The paper states only that "Roughly, consistency with observations requires that the axion luminosity La ... must not exceed the total neutrino luminosity Lν" and then applies this to exclude parameter space, but it does not discuss the statistical limitations of the sparse SN 1987A neutrino data; instead it later says "even the sparse observations of the SN 1987A neutrino burst can rule out..." without qualifying the criterion.

evidence.claim: The statement that axion luminosity must not exceed neutrino luminosity is based on a crude criterion and the manuscript fails to acknowledge the statistical limitations of the SN 1987A neutrino dataset.
evidence.excerpt: The statement that "consistency with observations requires that the axion luminosity $L_a$ … must not exceed the total neutrino luminosity $L_\nu$" should be qualified. This is a well-known but admittedly crude criterion... and recent work has stressed its limitations when applied to the modern, sparse SN 1987A neutrino dataset...

judge_panel.reason: The paper acknowledges the criterion is approximate: 'Roughly, consistency with observations requires that the axion luminosity $L_a$ … must not exceed the total neutrino luminosity $L_\nu$'. The word 'Roughly' signals awareness of the approximation, but no explicit discussion of the statistical limitations of the sparse SN 1987A neutrino dataset is provided. For a short proceedings paper this may be acceptable, making the verdict ambiguous.

The paper states only that "Roughly, consistency with observations requires that the axion luminosity La ... must not exceed the total neutrino luminosity Lν" and then applies this to exclude parameter space, but it does not discuss the statistical limitations of the sparse SN 1987A neutrino data; instead it later says "even the sparse observations of the SN 1987A neutrino burst can rule out..." without qualifying the criterion.

While the author notes that the luminosity criterion applies 'Roughly', the manuscript indeed adopts the constraint that 'the axion luminosity La ... must not exceed the total neutrino luminosity Lν' without deeply addressing the statistical limitations of the sparse SN 1987A dataset as flagged by the reviewer.

evidence.claim: The discussion in Sec. 3.2 is overly brief, lacking explanations for the low-energy SNe calorimetric bound and the rationale for why PVO supersedes SMM in part of parameter space.
evidence.excerpt: The discussion is somewhat rushed compared to Secs. 2 and 3.1. In particular: - The "low-energy SNe" calorimetric bound (Ref. 28) is mentioned but the underlying logic... is not explained. - The PVO vs. SMM discussion... is opaque; it is unclear to the reader why PVO supersedes SMM in part of the parameter space.

judge_panel.reason: The paper states the low-energy SNe argument 'rules out the region labeled Low-Energy SNe in Fig. 2' and the PVO/SMM discussion ends with 'these regions would be appropriately constrained by observations from the Pierre Venus Orbiter (PVO), rather than SMM', but neither the calorimetric logic nor the reason PVO supersedes SMM in part of the parameter space is explained for the reader.

Sec. 3.2 does explain the low-energy-SNe calorimetric logic: "If the energy deposition is too large, axion decays would power the ejection of the outer layers... it is necessary to conservatively require that the axion decays do not deposit an amount of energy larger than the explosion energy observed..." It also gives the PVO-vs-SMM rationale by noting that the photons can form a fireball and be "reprocessed from ∼ 100 MeV down to ∼ 100 keV," after which "these regions would be appropriately constrained by observations from the Pierre Venus Orbiter (PVO), rather than SMM 33."

The reviewer's claim that the underlying logic for the low-energy SNe bound is unexplained is factually incorrect. The text explicitly explains the calorimetric bound logic: 'If the energy deposition is too large, axion decays would power the ejection of the outer layers ... Thus, it is necessary to conservatively require that the axion decays do not deposit an amount of energy larger than the explosion energy ... low-energy SNe –a class with particularly low explosion energies– can severely constrain this scenario'.
